claim_reviews.conclusion: “Diabetes” matches the intended sense, though the wording is a general learner gloss rather than a clinical definition.
claim_reviews.subject: English cue and sense

claim_reviews.conclusion: Correct and standard in Indonesian; Indonesian health materials use diabetes/diabetes melitus for the chronic high-blood-sugar disease.
claim_reviews.subject: Indonesian answer: diabetes

claim_reviews.conclusion: Correct and established in Malaysian Malay; PRPM defines kencing manis as diabetes, and Malaysian Ministry of Health materials use the term.
claim_reviews.subject: Malaysian answer: kencing manis

claim_reviews.conclusion: Materially overstated. Malaysian Malay also accepts and uses diabetes, while Indonesian also uses kencing manis; official materials in both varieties explicitly pair the terms as equivalents. “Different-common-word” is therefore misleading unless qualified as a register or preference contrast.
claim_reviews.evidence_limitation: The sources establish acceptance and cross-variety overlap, but do not quantify which form is more frequent in everyday speech in each country.
claim_reviews.subject: National split and final relation

claim_reviews.conclusion: No false-friend contrast is supported: both expressions refer to the same disease, and the apparent difference is lexical/register preference rather than divergent meaning.
claim_reviews.evidence_limitation: No dedicated false-friend corpus analysis was located; the conclusion follows from dictionary equivalence and official health usage.
claim_reviews.subject: False-friend contrast

response.rationale: The forms are semantically correct, but the national split is materially overstated: “diabetes” and “kencing manis” are accepted equivalents in both Indonesian and Malaysian Malay. The relation should not be presented as a variety-exclusive different-common-word contrast. No false-friend contrast is warranted. Exact ordinary-frequency ranking by variety was not established.
